### Doggerland – the “dry‑land” of the North Sea

| Feature | What it is today | What existed during the last ice age (≈ 20 kyr ago) |
|---------|------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| **Body of water** | The southern North Sea (Dogger Bank, the North Sea basin) | An extensive tract of land—called **Doggerland**—which stretched from the east coast of England and Scotland out to the Netherlands, Denmark and even as far as northern France. |
| **Level change** | Sea level is now ~120 m higher than during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) | The drop in sea level (≈ 120 m) exposed the entire continental shelf of the North Sea, creating a wide plain, rivers, lakes and marshes. |
| **Geography** | Today a shallow sea with the Dogger Bank, shoals and an international maritime boundary. | A verdant, temperate landscape that connected Britain to mainland Europe. Picture an “island‑continent” that collapsed when the ice melted and sea level rose. |
| **Human use** | Modern shipping lane; no permanent land mass. | Archaeological evidence shows villages, agriculture, stone tool production, and even livestock grazing. Doggerland disappeared around 6 500–6 200 BCE as the post‑glacial sea level rise flooded the low‑lying plateau (the Storegga tsunami is one of the proposed drivers). |

**Why it matters:**  
Doggerland is the classic example of a major body of water that was **“dry land”** during the last ice age and only became the North Sea we know today after the winds of warming ripped the ice sheets away, raising sea level again.

**Other examples** (for context)  

| Body of water | Dry‑land equivalent during the LGM |
|---------------|------------------------------------|
| Baltic Sea | A large wetland system, largely covered by lakes and marshes, only a shallow lagoon connected to the North Sea. |
| Adriatic Sea (southern part) | Mostly terrestrial, with a shallow brackish lagoon at the river mouths. |
| Mediterranean (parts of the southern coast) | Drastically lower sea level exposed the Sahara, parts of the Sahara–Arabian Peninsula and the Nile delta were large floodplains. |

However, if you’re looking for a single widely‑known example besides the Irish Channel and the Atlantic near Kilkee, **Doggerland** is the most iconic and well‑documented, and it is often cited in academic and popular accounts of the Pleistocene landscape of northern Europe.
